title: Sequel to 'Scary Stories' Might Be Stuck in Legal Limbo!
summary:
Remember the movie 'Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark'? It came out in 2019 and was based on those creepy books with the terrifying drawings. Well, a sequel was announced back in 2020, and fans have been waiting ever since. The director, André Øvredal, says he has a story ready and he really wants to make it. But there's a big problem: the rights to the movie are stuck in what he calls 'copyright ownership hell.'

You see, the first movie was made by two studios: CBS Films and Entertainment One (eOne). But CBS Films shut down in 2019, and eOne was sold by Hasbro in 2022. So now, the rights are split between two companies that don't even exist anymore! Øvredal says the legal departments are trying to figure it out, but it's taking a long time. 'We have a story that I love that is just ready to go,' he said.

The first movie was a big hit, earning $104 million on a $25 million budget. Plus, it had Guillermo del Toro as a writer and producer. So a sequel seems like a no-brainer. But until the legal mess is sorted out, we'll just have to wait and hope. Fingers crossed!
why_it_matters: Even a popular movie can have a sequel canceled by legal puzzles, showing that every film depends on complicated business deals behind the scenes.

keywords.explanation: A sequel is a movie, book, or game that continues the story of an earlier one.
Copyright is a law that gives the creators of a work the right to control how it is used and who can make money from it.
Legal departments are teams of lawyers inside a company that handle law-related problems.
A no-brainer is something so obviously a good idea that it requires very little thinking to decide.
A budget is the amount of money planned to be spent on a project, like making a movie.
Guillermo del Toro is a famous Mexican film director and writer known for fantasy and horror movies.

Guillermo del Toro (the Mexican filmmaker behind 'Pan's Labyrinth' and 'The Shape of Water') helped write and produce the first movie.
When a company goes out of business or gets sold, the ownership of its movies can get tangled for years, which the director calls 'copyright ownership hell'.
Article_Structure: WHO: Director André Øvredal, the studios CBS Films and eOne, and waiting fans.
WHAT: The planned sequel to 'Scary Stories' is stuck because movie rights are split between companies that no longer exist.
WHERE: In the movie business—the first film was a worldwide hit.
WHY: CBS Films shut down and eOne was sold by Hasbro, leaving the rights in legal limbo.

perspectives.description: The director has a story he loves and Guillermo del Toro was involved before, so if the legal dust clears, the sequel could be just as scary and fun.
The original companies don't exist anymore, so the rights might stay frozen forever and the sequel could slowly die.
This is a frustrating but common problem in Hollywood: when studios merge or close, old movie rights get stuck and projects stall.
